1051.title: Sirhind victory day
1051.hook: in May, Sikhs mark Banda Singh Bahadur's victory at Chappar Chiri
1051.tomorrow: The ninth Guru and his three companions
1051.howItsDone: Sikhs mark the victory at Chappar Chiri with kirtan, Ardas and langar, and some gather at Chappar Chiri, where the battle was fought.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vadda Ghallughara, and your line was they shielded the families. Today the calendar turns from grief to victory, and asks how a victory should be kept.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh: the Khalsa belongs to Waheguru, and so does the victory. On one early-summer day, that greeting carries extra weight on a field on the road to Sirhind. Kirtan rises, steam lifts from the langar pots, and the sangat sits down together. This is Chappar Chiri, where Banda Singh Bahadur's army met the forces of Wazir Khan, the governor whose order had ended the lives of Guru Gobind Singh's youngest sons. Sikh memory waited a long time for that day. Now the field holds a fair.
screen: `THE VICTORY IS WAHEGURU'S.` → `A FIELD ON THE ROAD TO SIRHIND.` → `CHAPPAR CHIRI.`

segments.voice: This path has already stood on this field and walked into Sirhind with Banda Singh. Today's question is how the day is kept. In Sikh memory, the winter order at Sirhind was a wound that stayed open. When Wazir Khan fell at Chappar Chiri and the city was taken, that long wait ended. So the day is marked with joy, with kirtan and langar. But justice and revenge are not the same word. Revenge is about what I want back. Justice, in the Sikh telling, is about wrong being answered. The line is not we got even. It's justice came, and the victory, as the greeting says, belongs to Waheguru, not to any commander. There's a deeper court, too. In the Japji, Guru Nanak's morning prayer, the thirty-fourth stanza describes the realm of dharam, where, in paraphrase, each person is judged by their own deeds, and true is the One, and true is the court. On that view, no human victory is the last word. And the honest telling: historians record that the city's people suffered when Sirhind was taken. A fair account keeps that too. So the day is kept with joy, but it doesn't become a day to hate anyone living now. The boys in the tower aren't brought back by any battle. What came was justice, not repair.
screen: `A LONG WAIT ENDED.` · `JUSTICE IS NOT REVENGE.` · `JAPJI 34: JUDGED BY DEEDS.` · `THE HONEST TELLING.` · then, large: `JUSTICE CAME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one wrong you've seen, near or far, that hasn't been answered; it might be small, someone blamed for what they didn't do, or it might be large. Hold it without anger and ask what justice would look like here, not revenge, not getting even, just the wrong put right, and let the question sit without needing an answer. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and leave the rest to the true court.
Chappar Chiri. The field where Banda Singh Bahadur's army won the victory marked each year as Sirhind victory day, when a long wait for justice ended. Today's word.
Your line: justice came. The victory, as the greeting says, belongs to Waheguru. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1051 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE NINTH GURU AND HIS THREE COMPANIONS.`

1052.title: The ninth Guru and his three companions
1052.hook: Mati Das, Sati Das and Dayala are remembered with Guru Tegh Bahadur each year
1052.howItsDone: On the remembrance of Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom, Sikhs gather for kirtan and Ardas, including at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi, and remember Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala with him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chappar Chiri, and your line was justice came. Today, a day of memory that keeps a Guru and his friends together.

Strength is gone. I'm bound in chains. Nothing I do can help. That's the sense of a short salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and tradition links it to his imprisonment, before his death in Delhi. But he wasn't alone in that prison. Three men had come with him, and they were put to death before him, tradition says, to break him. Each year, when Sikhs remember the ninth Guru, those three names are said beside his.
screen: `STRENGTH IS GONE. BOUND IN CHAINS.` → `HE WASN'T ALONE.` → `THREE NAMES BESIDE HIS.`

segments.voice: Bhai Mati Das. His brother, Bhai Sati Das. And Bhai Dayala. This path met them in the story of Delhi: two brothers and a third companion, all close to the Guru. None of them was a Guru. Tradition says each was offered his life if he gave up his faith, and each refused. When Sikhs mark Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom, in gurdwaras and at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi, the three companions are remembered on the same day, beside him. The day belongs to a Guru and his friends. In the salok from today's opening, on Ang 1429, the ninth Guru says strength is gone and the chains are on, and then turns: now only the Lord is my support. The very next salok answers it: strength has come, the chains are broken, everything is possible, everything is in your hands. Tradition holds that this answer came from his son, Guru Gobind Singh, though readers differ on who wrote it. Either way, the two saloks sit side by side, like a conversation across a prison wall. Why three names and not one? A remembrance that kept only the leader would lose the people who stood next to him. In the story, the Guru was not alone in the worst room of his life, and the day doesn't let anyone forget who was there with him.
screen: `THREE NAMES, NONE OF THEM GURUS.` · `REMEMBERED ON THE SAME DAY.` · `CHAINS, AND THE ANSWER: ANG 1429.` · `NOT THE LEADER ALONE.` · then, large: `THREE COMPANIONS.`

segments.voice: Set out three small things in a row, three stones, three coins, three cups, and with each one say a name, aloud or inside: Mati Das, Sati Das, Dayala. Then sit with all three in front of you, breathe slowly, and let them stand, too, for the people who have stood beside you in a hard room. If you pray, you can say Waheguru.
Bhai Dayala. One of the three companions of Guru Tegh Bahadur, with Bhai Mati Das and Bhai Sati Das, who would not give up their faith. Today's word.
Your line: three companions. Three names, always said beside his. That's day one thousand fifty-two.

1053.title: The Sahibzade week
1053.hook: late December, Sikhs remember all four sons and Mata Gujri, some sleeping on the floor
1053.howItsDone: In late December, Sikhs remember the Sahibzade and Mata Gujri with kirtan, langar and the Shaheedi Jor Mela at Fatehgarh Sahib. Some families keep the week simply at home: no celebrations, and sleeping on the floor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Dayala, and your line was three companions. Today, the remembrance moves to the Guru's own family, in the cold of winter.

In some Sikh homes in late December, the mattress comes off the bed and goes onto the floor. A thin blanket. The heater turned down. No parties, no sweets. Children who'd normally be counting down to a holiday are told a story instead, the same story, night after night. It's the week Sikhs remember the Sahibzade, the sons of Guru Gobind Singh, and their grandmother, Mata Gujri.
screen: `A MATTRESS ON THE FLOOR.` → `NO PARTIES, NO SWEETS.` → `THE SAME STORY, NIGHT AFTER NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sahibzade means the sons of the Guru's house, and this week keeps all four together with their grandmother. This path told their stories one by one; today, side by side. The elder sons, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, fell fighting at Chamkaur. The younger sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were held with Mata Gujri in the cold tower at Sirhind, refused to give up their faith, and were put to death. Tradition says their grandmother died in the tower. So the week holds a battlefield and a tower, in the same cold season. At Fatehgarh Sahib the Shaheedi Jor Mela gathers crowds; at home, the week is quieter. Tradition says that after Chamkaur, alone in the forest of Machhiwara, Guru Gobind Singh composed a short song to the beloved friend, kept in the Dasam Granth. One line says, in paraphrase, that a bed of straw with the friend is good, and living in comfortable homes without him is like living in a furnace. The Guru, having lost so much, chooses the hard ground with the friend over comfort without him. Families who sleep on the floor this week aren't punishing themselves. They're keeping company with a grandmother and two boys in a cold tower, and a father sleeping rough in a forest. For a few nights, comfort steps aside so the memory has room.
screen: `FOUR SONS AND A GRANDMOTHER.` · `CHAMKAUR, AND THE COLD TOWER.` · `A STRAW BED WITH THE FRIEND.` · `WHY THE FLOOR?` · then, large: `THE COLD WEEK.`

segments.voice: Some night this week, if you choose, you might give up one small comfort before sleep, a lighter blanket, no screen in bed, the heater lower, nothing harmful or extreme; for now, just choose which it would be. Then feel the floor or the chair under you holding you, breathe slowly, and remember the four boys and their grandmother for a minute. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them.

1054.title: Maghi: the torn letter
1054.hook: at Muktsar the story of the forty and their torn letter is told again
1054.howItsDone: On Maghi, Sikhs gather at Sri Muktsar Sahib to bathe in the pool, visit the town's gurdwaras and hear kirtan, and the story of the Chali Mukte and the torn disclaimer is retold. Gurdwaras elsewhere also remember them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sahibzade, and your line was the cold week. Today, the calendar moves into the new year, and a winter fair keeps a story about a piece of paper.

The sound of paper tearing is small. A quick rip, and it's done. But Sikh memory has kept one tear for a very long time. At Muktsar, in Punjab, on the winter day called Maghi, crowds come to the pool and the gurdwaras of the town, and the story is told again: Sikhs who signed a paper walking away from their Guru, then came back and fell in battle, and the Guru who tore that paper up.
screen: `A SMALL SOUND.` → `CROWDS AT MUKTSAR.` → `THE STORY TOLD AGAIN.`

segments.voice: During the siege of Anandpur, tradition says, a band of Sikhs asked to go home, and the Guru asked them to write it down. They signed a disclaimer, the bedava: you are not our Guru, we are not your Sikhs. A paper is a record. It can outlast the mood that wrote it. Shamed and stirred by Mai Bhago, the same men rode back and fell at Khidrana, defending the Guru. Tradition says one of them, Mahan Singh, was still alive when the Guru reached him, and asked for one thing: tear up the paper. The Guru tore it. The record was gone. The relationship was whole. The Ardas names them as the Chali Mukte, the liberated ones, and tradition ties the town's name, Muktsar, to them. On Ang 1372, Bhagat Kabir says, in paraphrase, that where there is wisdom there is dharam, where there is falsehood there is sin, where there is greed there is death, and where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord himself. On that reading, the Guru's tear wasn't a small kindness at the end of a battle. It was the Lord's own presence in a torn page. Maghi could have been a day about loyalty, about the ones who never left. Instead, the story it tells is about people who left, came back, and were forgiven.
screen: `A PAPER THAT SAID GOODBYE.` · `THE GURU TORE IT.` · `WHERE THERE IS FORGIVENESS.` · `MAGHI KEEPS THE TEAR.` · then, large: `THE LETTER TORN.`

segments.voice: On any scrap of paper, a receipt or a sticky note, write a word or two that stands for an old grudge you've kept; nobody will see it. Hold it for a breath, then tear it slowly in half, and in half again, knowing you don't have to feel finished with it, since tearing is only a start. Set the pieces aside and breathe slowly, and if you pray, you can say Waheguru.

1055.title: Hola: the Nihang parade
1055.hook: the Nihang dals ride and display gatka at Anandpur
1055.howItsDone: At Hola Mohalla in Anandpur Sahib, Nihang Singh dals ride in procession with horses and flags, display horsemanship and gatka, and the gathering includes kirtan and langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maghi, and your line was the letter torn. Today the calendar turns to spring, and to a loud, happy day of memory.

Hooves on hard ground, and a roar from the crowd. A rider in deep blue leans out of the saddle at a gallop and lifts something from the dirt with the tip of a spear. Behind him come more riders, tall turbans, flags snapping on long poles, drums. On the edge of the field, two young men circle each other with sticks and small shields, laughing between blows. This is Anandpur Sahib at Hola Mohalla, and the riders are the Nihang Singhs.
screen: `HOOVES AND A ROAR.` → `RIDERS IN DEEP BLUE.` → `ANANDPUR SAHIB.`

segments.voice: This path has met Hola Mohalla, gatka and the Nihangs, each on its own day. Today, the parade as a day of memory. The Nihang Singhs are organized in bands called dals, and at Hola they come to Anandpur with their horses, flags and old weapons, and ride in procession through the town and out onto the open ground. It's a parade, not a war. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh called the Sikhs together at Anandpur for drills and mock battles, turning the spring season of Holi toward courage. The Nihangs keep that memory the way it was given: as play with a purpose. The horsemanship is real and the skill hard won, but the mood is a festival, not a threat. In the dust, pairs spar at gatka with stick and shield, footwork first, eyes on the partner. Children watch and copy. A skill that could have been lost is passed on in public, in joy. In the Dasam Granth, in a hymn often sung as Deh Shiva, Guru Gobind Singh asks, in paraphrase, for one boon: that he never turn back from doing good. It's a prayer for courage, and Sikhs sing it at gatherings. The parade gives that prayer a body: people who ride forward, not back, and do it laughing. Memory doesn't always have to be quiet. Sometimes it gallops.
screen: `THE DALS RIDE OUT.` · `A PARADE, NOT A WAR.` · `GATKA, PASSED ON IN PUBLIC.` · `DEH SHIVA: NEVER TURN BACK.` · then, large: `RIDE IN JOY.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand and shake out your hands, arms and shoulders, then march in place a few steps with your knees a little high, and let it be a bit silly, smiling if you can. Take three strong breaths, in through the nose and out through the mouth, then sit and feel your heart going, joy and strength in the same body. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each breath as it slows.
Hola. The spring days at Anandpur Sahib when the Nihang dals ride in procession and gatka is played in public, memory kept in motion. Today's word.
Your line: ride in joy. Deh Shiva asks: never turn back from doing good. See you tomorrow.

1056.title: Vaisakhi: 1699, 1919 and today
1056.hook: one day that holds the Khalsa's birth, a massacre, and a harvest
1056.howItsDone: On Vaisakhi, Sikhs gather in gurdwaras for kirtan and Ardas, celebrate the founding of the Khalsa with nagar kirtan processions and langar, and in Punjab mark the wheat harvest. In Amritsar, people also visit the Jallianwala Bagh memorial.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hola, and your line was ride in joy. Today the calendar of memory comes to a day that gathers several of this year's stories at once.

Three scenes, one day. In the fields, wheat falls to the sickle. In the gurdwaras, Sikhs sing the birthday of the Khalsa. And in Amritsar, some people stand quietly in a walled garden. Guru Nanak has a line in the Asa di Var that sounds strange on a festival: suffering became the medicine, and comfort the disease. Vaisakhi is a day that can hold it. Today's title carries two years and a word: the year tradition gives for the Khalsa's birth, the year of the garden, and today.
screen: `THREE SCENES, ONE DAY.` → `SUFFERING, THE MEDICINE.` → `TWO YEARS AND A WORD.`

segments.voice: This path has spent whole days on each of these. Today, hold them in one hand. First, birth. At Anandpur, on Vaisakhi, Guru Gobind Singh called for those who would give their heads, and the five beloved stood up. The amrit was stirred, and the Khalsa was born. That's the first year in the title, the date tradition gives. Then grief. On a Vaisakhi much later, troops fired on an unarmed gathering in Jallianwala Bagh, the garden this path stood in a week ago. That's the second year. Then harvest. Long before either, Vaisakhi was the harvest day in Punjab, and tradition says Guru Amar Das asked the Sikhs to gather at Vaisakhi. The harvest comes every year, whatever else happened. That's the last word in the title: today. Why can one day hold all three? On Ang 469, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that suffering became the medicine and comfort the disease, because when there is comfort, the One is forgotten. He isn't praising pain. On one reading, hardship can keep the One in mind, where comfort lets the One slip away. So on Vaisakhi, the harvest and the birth are celebrated fully, and the grief is not pushed out of the room. Joy without memory would forget the garden. Memory without joy would forget the Khalsa's birthday and the wheat. The same day holds kirtan, langar, processions, and, in Amritsar, silence in a garden.

segments.voice: On the first long breath, bring to mind something newly born in your life, a friendship, a habit, an idea, and give thanks for it; on the next, something you've lost, not to reopen it, but to give thanks that you were able to love it. On the third, give thanks for something ready, a harvest: work finished, a season you came through. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after each one, then rest with all three.
Vaisakhi. The day that holds the Khalsa's birth, the grief of Jallianwala Bagh, and the harvest, all at once. Today's word.
Your line: birth, grief, harvest. All three can be true on one day. That's day one thousand fifty-six.

1057.title: Looking back: tellers and saints
1057.hook: Bhai Gurdas, the janamsakhis and fifteen Bhagats
1057.howItsDone: Sikhs hear the vars of Bhai Gurdas sung in kirtan alongside Gurbani, retell the janamsakhi stories of Guru Nanak at gurpurabs and to children, and sing the Bhagats' hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib as part of the Guru's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vaisakhi, one day holding three things: birth, grief, harvest. Today the year starts folding up behind us.

Every story you've heard this year reached you because somebody told it first. A scribe bent over a page with a reed pen. A storyteller in a village courtyard, saying, and then Baba Nanak went on to the next town. A weaver at his loom, singing to God, whose song ended up in the Guru's own book. Before the battles and the kingdoms, year three began with these people, the ones who carried the story. For the last days of the year, this path turns around to look at the road. First, the tellers and the saints.
screen: `SOMEBODY TOLD IT FIRST.` → `A SCRIBE, A STORYTELLER, A WEAVER.` → `TURNING AROUND ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Start with the scribe. Tradition says Bhai Gurdas wrote out the Adi Granth in his own hand for Guru Arjan. He also wrote vars of his own: long poems in pauris, each with a picture and a point. He tells Nanak's journeys, the yogis on the mountain, the qazis at Mecca, the Guru laying down the pilgrim's robe to live as a householder. Tradition says Guru Arjan called those vars the key to the Guru's word. Next, the storytellers. The janamsakhis, the birth-stories of Nanak, came down in more than one family of tellings: the Puratan, the Bala, Miharban's reflective version, an illustrated one. They don't always agree on the details. Some readers take them as memory and devotion more than as diaries, and that's part of what they teach: a life so loved that people kept telling it, each in their own voice. Then the saints. At the end of the ragas in the Guru Granth Sahib sit the hymns of the Bhagats. Kabir. Shaikh Farid, the Sufi. Namdev. Ravidas, who in his own hymns names the low caste he was born into and says the Name lifted him anyway. Dhanna the farmer, Sain the barber, and others. They came from many places and castes, from Hindu and Muslim backgrounds, and the Gurus set their words beside their own. One shape runs through all three: the Gurus' word didn't travel alone. It traveled in the hands of people who wrote, retold and sang it. The tellers.
screen: `THE SCRIBE: BHAI GURDAS AND HIS VARS.` · `THE STORYTELLERS: THE JANAMSAKHIS.` · `THE SAINTS: BHAGATS IN THE GURU'S BOOK.` · `THE WORD TRAVELS IN HUMAN HANDS.` · then, large: `THE TELLERS.`

segments.voice: Let one teller from this year step forward: the scribe with his careful pen, Bhai Nand Lal with his Persian verses of longing, Kabir at the loom, Farid, or the unnamed people who first said, and then Baba Nanak went on. Hold that person in mind for a few breaths, and say their name quietly. If you pray, say Waheguru in thanks for them on each breath out.
Looking back. Turning at the end of the year to see the road: today, the scribe, the storytellers and the saints whose words sit in the Guru's book. Today's word.
Your line: the tellers. A story lives as long as someone keeps telling it. Thanks for sitting with me.
